'''Fukura Tenmangū''' (福良天満宮) is a [[Shinto shrine]] ([[Tenmangū]]) located in [[Usuki, Ōita]], Japan. It enshrines [[Sugawara no Michizane]], the deity commonly known as "Tenjin-sama."

== History ==
After [[Sugawara no Michizane]] was exiled to [[Dazaifu (government)|Dazaifu, Fukuoka]] and passed away in 903 ([[Engi (era)]] 3), his descendants took the surname Ohata and continued to protect his image in [[Suō Province]]. During the [[Tenshō (Momoyama period)|Tenshō Era]] period (circa 1590), they fled from Toyotomi Hideyoshi's national unification campaigns and brought the enshrined deity to [[Kaifu District, Bungo Province]], Fukura Manor.<ref name="about">{{Cite web|title=History|publisher=Fukura Tenmangū|url=http://fukuragu.jp/wp/about|accessdate=2018-12-20}}</ref>

In the early [[Keichō]] era (circa 1600), Monk Enyo established [[Ryūgen-ji]] at Tairashimizu and Shōmyō-ji in Fukura Village.<ref name="about" />

In 1602 (Keichō 13), [[Inaba Sadamichi]], lord of Usuki Castle, lost a hawk during a hunt. After praying at a small shrine at the foot of Chinzan Mountain, the hawk returned to a pine tree nearby. In gratitude, he relocated the shrine, first to Miyabata and later to its current location within Shōmyō-ji, naming it "Yotaka-den" (呼鷹殿).<ref name="about" />

Shōmyō-ji later converted to [[Shingon Buddhism]], received the title Sugiōin from [[Ninna-ji]], and was successively renamed Sugashōin Tenman-ji, Bairinzan Tenman-ji, and finally Zuiō-in Tenman-ji under [[Tiantai|Tendai Buddhism]]. The shrine received patronage from the [[Inaba clan]], who revered Sugawara no Michizane.<ref name="about" />

In 1868 ([[Meiji Restoration]]), following the [[Shinbutsu bunri]], it was renamed Tenman Shrine. In 1895 (Meiji 28), the current main hall was constructed.<ref name="about" />

During the [[Shōwa era]], the shrine was renamed Fukura Tenmangū. In 1982 (Shōwa 57), it was used as a filming location for "[[Otoko wa Tsurai yo: Hana mo Arashi mo Torajirō]]."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Torasan filming location|publisher=Fukura Tenmangū|url=http://fukuragu.jp/tora|accessdate=2018-12-20}}</ref> In 2002 (Heisei 14), the 1100th anniversary festival of Sugawara no Michizane was held.

== Festivals ==
A summer festival is held for three days in late July, featuring [[Kagura]] performances and Akajishi-ren (red lion dance).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Fukura Tenmangū Summer Festival|publisher=Tourism Oita|url=https://www.visit-oita.jp/events/detail/9595/|accessdate=2018-12-20}}</ref> The third day features a mikoshi procession and a popular "Yakumo-harai" (serpent exorcism) ritual. It is one of Usuki's three major summer festivals.<ref name="event07">{{Cite web|title=Summer Festival|publisher=Fukura Tenmangū|url=http://fukuragu.jp/event/event07|accessdate=2018-12-20}}</ref>

== Subordinate Shrines ==
* '''{{nihongo|Yuga Shrine|瑜伽神社}}''' – Enshrines [[Ame-no-Tajikarao]] and [[Shirafuji-no-Tayū]].<ref name="event07" /> A branch shrine of [[Yuga Shrine (Kurashiki)]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Fukura Tenmangū Summer Festival|publisher=Kurashiki Yuga Shrine|url=http://www.yugasan.or.jp/gyoujihoukoku/2011/2011fukura/fukura2011.html|accessdate=2018-12-20}}</ref>
* '''Atago Shrine''' – Enshrines [[Ukemochi]] and [[Kagu-tsuchi]].<ref name="event07" />
* '''Okunomiya Akameko Shrine''' – Built in 1999 (Heisei 11). Hosts the Usuki Akameko Festival in early May.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Usuki Akameko Festival|publisher=Fukura Tenmangū|url=http://fukuragu.jp/event/event05|accessdate=2018-12-20}}</ref>
